title: No work, no food
hook: the Chan master Baizhang: a day without work is a day without food (Chan tradition)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was right livelihood, the Buddha's short list of trades to leave alone. Your line was harm into the hands of someone else. Today, a teacher who wouldn't stop working.
screen: `HARM INTO THE HANDS OF SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: The tools are gone. The hoe, the rake, whatever he used in the fields, hidden by his own students. They meant well. Their teacher was old, the Chan tradition says, and still went out every day to work the land beside the monks, and they wanted him to rest. He didn't argue. He didn't search. He just didn't eat that day. When they asked why, his answer has been passed down in Chan and Zen communities: a day without work is a day without food. The teacher was Baizhang. Today's word is the first half of his saying.
screen: `THE TOOLS ARE HIDDEN.` → `HE DOESN'T EAT.` → `A DAY WITHOUT WORK.`

segments.voice: First, who Baizhang is in the story. Chan is the Chinese school of Buddhism known in Japan as Zen. Tradition remembers Baizhang as a Chan master who shaped how a monastery ran day to day: when to sit, when to eat, when to work. In this telling, the monks didn't only meditate. They farmed, cooked, swept and hauled, and the teacher worked with them. Second, what the saying is not. No work, no food can sound like a threat a boss might shout. But in the story, Baizhang says it of himself. Nobody punishes him; he simply keeps his own rule. The sharpness is aimed inward. Third, a difference worth saying plainly. In other Buddhist communities, monks live on alms, food given by lay people, and that giving is itself a practice for the givers. The Chan way of working the land grew up alongside that, as a different arrangement, not a correction of it. Both keep a community fed and a mind awake. Fourth, what it might mean at a kitchen table. In a monastery, work is shared, and nobody's job is beneath anyone. Somebody washes the pots, and the teacher might be the one with his sleeves rolled up. At home, the same question waits by the sink. Baizhang's saying doesn't ask you to earn your dinner in money. It asks whether you've done your share of what keeps the place running.
screen: `A CHAN MASTER IN THE FIELDS.` · `A RULE HE KEPT FOR HIMSELF.` · `ALMS, OR THE HOE: BOTH FEED.` · `YOUR SHARE AT HOME.` · then, large: `NO WORK, NO FOOD.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you wish others at home would do, rinse the cup, put the shoes away, and notice the small heat of that wish without scolding it. Then turn it around, the way Baizhang did: make it a quiet rule for you alone, just for today, told to nobody, and hold it while the breath comes and goes. If you pray, you can bring your household into it in your own tradition's words.
No work. The first half of Baizhang's saying, a day without work is a day without food: a rule he kept for himself. Today's word.
Your line: sleeves rolled up. The teacher, too, washing the pots beside everyone. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Chan and Zen monasteries, monks and teachers share manual work such as cooking, cleaning and gardening as part of daily practice, and Baizhang's saying is often quoted about it.

chat.says: 'A day without work, a day without food' sounds harsh. Who was that teacher being hard on?
options: Himself. When his tools were hidden, Baizhang just didn't eat; nobody punished him.
His monks. He took away their meals whenever they skipped a day in the fields.
Lazy people in town. He said they didn't deserve alms unless they farmed.
chat.meaning: In the story, Baizhang says it of himself and simply keeps his own rule. The sharpness is aimed inward.

notes: The hidden-tools story and the saying are told as Chan tradition, not as documented fact. A Buddhist Keeper should confirm the framing and name the classical source (e.g. later Chan records) if wanted.

'Tradition remembers Baizhang as a Chan master who shaped how a Chan monastery ran' refers to the monastic rules traditionally credited to him; their authorship is debated by historians. Confirm phrasing.

'In other Buddhist communities, monks live on alms' is a general description not stated by a cited text; a Keeper should confirm it. 'Chan ... later traveled to Japan as Zen' is likewise uncited general history; confirm.
Chinese 一日不作，一日不食 and pinyin yi ri bu zuo, yi ri bu shi: confirm characters and the pronunciation guide.
Alms and field work are presented as two arrangements, neither ranked.
